titleStmt.title: Exact Response Time Analysis of Hierarchical Fixed-Priority Scheduling

analytic.title: Exact Response Time Analysis of Hierarchical Fixed-Priority Scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.head: Hierarchical scheduling has recently been used to provide temporal isolation to embedded virtualised systems.
div.p: Response time analysis is a common way to derive a schedulability test for these systems. This paper points out that response time analysis for hierarchical fixed-priority scheduling found in the literature is only exact for tasks of the highest priority domain. For the rest of the tasks is an upper bound. In our work, we provide the exact analysis and we compare it with previously published works.

div.head: I. Introduction
div.p: In the last years, embedded systems have increased its processing capabilities and its computational resources in such a way that they are capable of executing several concurrent real-time applications that would formerly have required several embedded systems. Scheduling several applications on a single processor not only reduces cost but assures better reliability, because the overall complexity of the system is reduced [1]. The design of such systems can be solved by means of virtualization, where the processor is subdivided in multiple domains, each of them with its own operating system and applications running on top. Switching between domains is the role of an hypervisor. When the virtualization technique is used in real-time embedded systems, the performance plays the most important role. Most of the recent advances on virtualization has been done in the desktop systems. Transferring these results to embedded systems is not as direct as it may seem. Example of a recent real-time hypervisor is XtratuM [2].

Hierarchical scheduling has recently been used to provide temporal isolation to these systems. In a hierarchical system, the hypervisor is in charge of domain scheduling, also called the global scheduler. On the second level, This work was partially supported by Spanish Government Research Office under grant DPI2008-06737-C02-02, TIN2008-06766-C03-02/TIN and by ITEA2 programme under TECOM project (FIT-340005-2007-40) the local scheduler schedules domain's tasks. In recent years, considerable effort has been made in order to provide exact schedulability analysis to hierarchical systems. Specifically, for fixed-priority hierarchical systems (where fixed-priority scheduling policy is used in both global and local schedulers) the work by Davis and Burns [3] provides an exact worst case response time analysis. The aim of our work is to point out that this analysis is not always exact, and we will provide the exact formulation.

The organisation of the paper is as follows: section II presents the most important works in the field of hierarchical scheduling. Section III presents the model and notation used, while in section IV the analysis of Davis and Burns is introduced. The exact worst case response time of tasks under a two-level hierarchical scheme for fixed-priority is presented in section V. In section VI, we evaluate the exact analysis presented in this work by comparing it with Davis and Burns analysis. Finally, section VII summarises the contributions of the paper and future lines of work.

div.head: II. Related work
div.p: Hierarchical scheduling has been a topic of research interest in recent years. One of the first works on this area is the one presented by Deng and Liu [4], based on a twolevel real-time scheduling framework. Kuo and Li [5] presented an exact schedulability condition for this framework assuming fixed priority pre-emptive scheduling. Lipari and Baruah [6] presented a similar work with EDF. Saewong et al. [7] provided a response time analysis for fixedpriority hierarchical systems. This analysis was pessimistic as it was showed by Davis and Burns in [3]. Almeida and Pedreiras [8] improved the analysis by Saewong et al. but, again it was not an exact analysis. In [9], Bril et al. show that the worst case response time of a task is not necessarily assumed for the first job with the conditions of critical instant provided by Davis and Burns. They claim that the existing analysis could be improved but they do not provide an alternative analysis. Lipari and Bini [10] provide a kind of sensitivity analysis of the global level for a two-level hierarchical system, providing a methodology for calculating the domain parameters that makes the task set feasible.

div.head: III. System model and notation
div.p: Our model is concerned with the pre-emptive scheduling of real-time applications on an uniprocessor. Each application consists of a number of real-time domains or partitions 1 . Each domain comprises a number of tasks. Thus, our hierarchical system has two levels, the domain level and the task level, each of them with its own scheduling policy. In this work, we will assume that both levels are scheduling with a fixed-priority scheduling policy. Domains D s are characterised by its budget C s and replenishment period T s . Tasks T si of a domain D s are characterised by its worst case computation time C si , relative deadline D si and period T si . We will assume Periodic Server or Deferrable Server policy for the hypervisor (global level). In Periodic Server policy, if a domain still has not consumed its budget and there are no active tasks to consume it, the budget is consumed as if there was a background task always ready to execute. This is opposed to the Deferrable Server policy, in which a domain can preserve its unused capacity until the end of its period. We will also assume that both tasks and domains are arranged in descending priority, that is, ∀x < s prio(D x ) > prio(D s ) and ∀i < j prio(T si ) > prio(T s j ).

div.head: IV. Davis and Burns analysis
div.p: Davis and Burns [3] characterise the worst case scenario in which the worst case response time of a task T si of domain D s is produced as:

Rule 1The domain D s has exhausted its capacity early in its period as possible. For Deferrable Server, the capacity has to be consumed by lower priority tasks. For Periodic server, the domain can consume its capacity even when there are not active tasks. Rule 2T si and all higher priority tasks of domain D s arrive just after the domain's capacity has been exhausted. Rule 3Once the domain replenishes its capacity, it suffers the most possible interference from higher priority domains. According to these rules, Davis and Burns characterised the worst case response time of a task T si as WCRT si = w n si + J s . The term J s = T s -C s is the release jitter of T si 1 also referred in the literature as servers relative to the release of its domain D s , whereas w n si is solved by a recurrence relation:
div.formula: w n si = L(w n si ) + G(w n si ) + I(w n si )(1)
div.p: where: L(w n si ): The load at ith priority level. It is calculated as:
div.formula: L(w n si ) = C si + ∑ ∀ j≤i w n si + J s T s j C s j (2)
div.p: G(w n si ): The gaps when the processor is not executing the domain of interest (D s ). It is given by:
div.formula: G(w n si ) = L(w n si ) C s -1 (T s -C s )(3)
div.p: I(w n si ): The interference of higher priority domains in the last domain period:
div.formula: I(w n si ) = ∑ ∀x≤s ⎡ ⎢ ⎢ ⎢ max 0, w n si - L(w n si ) C s -1 T s + J x T x ⎤ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ C x (4)
div.p: where J x is the release jitter of the higher priority domain D x . For a Deferrable Server J x = T x -C x , for a Periodic Server, J x = 0.
In [3], it is stated that the previous expression gives the exact worst case response time for T si . However, in the next counterexample, we will show that this is not always true.

div.head: A. Counterexample
div.p: The next example will illustrate that Davis and Burns analysis is an upper bound of the worst case response time of a task that belongs to a lower priority domain. Let's consider two domains, scheduled under the Periodic Server policy, whose parameters are listed in Table I. Task parameters of D 2 are listed in Table II. The execution chronogram of the system is depicted in Figure 1. In the bottom of the figure is represented the chronogram of the domain level, whereas in the top of the figure is depicted the chronogram of tasks belonging to domain D 2 . Execution of tasks belonging to D 1 has been omitted, since does not affect the execution of tasks of D 22 . As it can be seen in Figure 1, task 2 of domain 2 (T 22 ) presents a response time in its first activation of 30 units of time. We are interested in the worst case response time of this task. The analysis of Davis and Burns obtains a worst case response time of 73 (62 + 11). This worst case response time occurs at the first activation of the task in the worst case scenario [3]. Table III We are now interested on generating the worst case scenario, in order to depict the execution chronogram of this scenario and check if the worst case response time of T 22 is 73. Taking into account rule 2 defined in section IV, tasks T 21 and T 22 must activate just when D 2 has exhausted its budget as early as possible. For this reason, in the rest of the figures of this example, tasks T 21 and T 22 activate at instant t = 9. As far as rule 1 is concerned, D 1 has to arrive after D 2 has exhausted its budget, otherwise the condition "as early as possible" is not fulfilled. This situation is reproduced in Figure 2, where D 1 is activated at time t = 9. We can see that response time in the first activation of T 22 has raised to 40 (49-9), but it is still far from 73.

As the worst case response time of Davis and Burns does not coincide with the first response time of the generated scenario, we can think that we have not correctly generated the worst case scenario. This is true, because we have not taking into account rule 3 of the worst case scenario, which states that further execution of D 2 is delayed as long as possible due to the interference of higher priority domains. This takes us directly to the question: how much after D 2 exhausted its budget must arrive D 1 in order to cause the maximum interference? In Figure 2, D 1 arrives at instant 9, just to assure that D 2 has exhausted its budget, but can D 1 arrive a little bit later in order to accomplish rule 3 and produce the worst case response time in the first activation? In Figure 2, we can see that if D 1 is delayed three more units of time, it preempts D 2 in its last period (t = 40), so the second activation of T 21 preempts T 22 . Then, T 22 must wait until T 21 finishes its second activation making its response time considerably greater. Figure 3 shows this scenario, where the response time of T 22 raises to 72.

We have not found in the literature exactly when higher priority domains have to activate in order to produce the higher interference to accomplish rule 3. However, in Figure 3, we can observe that D 1 does not interfer in the last period of D 2 . This is the reason why the response time of T 22 in Figure 3 is 72, and if we consider that D 1 preempts D 2 in its last period, then the response time raises to 72+1=73, which is the worst case response time calculated by Davis and Burns. This means that D 1 must be released at time 80, therefore, it must arrive at t=10 in order to produce the worst case response time. Figure 4 shows the execution chronogram for D 1 arrival at t=10. However, contrary to all expectations, the response time not only does not increase to 73 but decreases to 40. The reason is that, as a result of moving D 1 , it does not preempt D 2 at time 40, therefore T 22 can finish its execution before the second activation of T 21 . Therefore, in order to obtain the worst case response time of T 22 , D 1 must preempt D 2 both in times 40 and 80. However, this is not possible due to the activation rates of D 1 .

As a conclusion, the analysis by Davis and Burns is not exact but an upper bound. This is due to the overestimation of the term I(w n i ). In the formulation of w n si , it is considered that higher priority domains cause the maximum interference in every activation of D s , but it does not have to be true, as this example illustrates. However, Davis and Burns analysis is exact for tasks belonging to the highest priority domain, since for these tasks I(w n si ) = 0.

div.head: V. Exact worst case response time
div.p: In order to obtain the exact worst case response time is mandatory to generate the worst case scenario, that is, to determine the arrivals of higher priority domains. To do this, we will add to both levels of the system model defined in section III an extra parameter: the offset. Thus: To calculate the worst case response time of T si , we will identify the worst case scenario, by means of applying different offsets to domains and tasks and we will reformulate equation 4 to calculate the exact interference of higher priority domains.

div.head: A. Worst case scenario
div.p: To calculate the exact worst case response time of a task T si , we will need to reproduce the worst case scenario applying different offsets to higher priority domains and tasks. For tasks, the worst case scenario is produced for the following offsets:

div.p: Lower priority domains will not preempt D s , so can have any arbitrary offset. Higher priority domains have to cause the highest interference after the first activation of D s but, as showed in the example of the previous section, we do not know exactly which are the offsets that generate the worst case. Therefore, the exact worst case response time must be calculated for different combinations of offsets of higher priority domains. The set of offsets of higher priority domains are:
div.formula: ∀x ≤ s O x ∈ [T s , T s + T x -1]
div.p: Therefore, the number of scenarios in which the worst case response time of T si may occur are: ∑ ∀x≤s T x . This implies that the calculation of the worst case response time consists of calculating the first response time of task T si in all these scenarios. To do this, we have to correct the term I(w n si ) to calculate the exact interference of higher priority domains. This re-defined term will be called I (w n si ). It is important to note that the term I (w n si ) will depend on higher priority domain parameters, and now we have to take into account the offset parameter. To calculate the exact interference I (w n si ) we can only do it by finding the busy period in which the last period of D s falls. To do this, we will split the time in a set of busy periods, [t i start ,t i end ], defined by Ripoll et al in [11] as follows:
div.formula: t i start = ⎧ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎩ i = 0 0 i > 0 minimum t such that t > t i-1
div.p: end and processor is not idle
div.formula: t i end = min t, t = ∑ C j ⎡ ⎢ ⎢ ⎢ t - t i start T i T i T j ⎤ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ and t > t i start
div.p: We want to identify the busy period in which the last period of domain D s is executed. We are interested then, in the first level scheduling, that is, the scheduling at the domain level, to identify exactly the interference of higher priority domains. This is the reason why in the above expression of the busy periods, period and computation parameters have only one subindex, because they refer to domain parameters. We also need to know which is the last domain period A n si . It can be calculated as:
div.formula: A n si = L(w n si ) C s -1 T s
div.p: which is the load L(w n si ) expanded with D s rate. Let [t start ,t end ] be the busy period in which A n si lies, that is, it holds that t start ≤ A n si < t end . We will calculate the interference of higher priority domains as:
div.formula: I (w n si ) = ∑ ∀x≤s C x ⎡ ⎢ ⎢ ⎢ max 0, w n si -A n si -t start -O x T x + O x -t start + J x T x ⎤ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥(5)

div.head: B. Characterisation of the worst case response time
div.p: The worst case response time of a task T si is defined as WCRT si = w n si + J s where:
div.formula: w n si = L(w n si ) + G(w n si ) + I (w n si )(6)
div.p: and L(w n si ), G(w n si ) and I (w n si ) were defined in equations 2, 3 and 5. Note that the offset of higher priority domains appears in I (w n si ) term, and as O x appears in the ceil function, solving the value of O x that maximises I (w n si ) is not direct. We must find the maximum value of I (w n si ) in order to calculate the maximum interference of higher priority domains that states rule 3. Therefore, the calculation of WCRT si must be made for all different offsets of higher priority domains, being WCRT si = max(w n si )
. Note that the cost of the worst case response time calculation has increased with respect to Davis and Burns analysis, specifically ∑ ∀x>s T x times.

div.head: C. Example
div.p: We will use the example explained in section IV-A, to see that the worst case response time of task T 22 is 72 instead of 73. The number of scenarios to test is 14. This scenario has the same parameters for domain D 2 and its tasks, and for domain D 1 the offset is the first value in the range [20,33], that is, O 1 = 20. div.head: VI. Simulations
div.p: This section will evaluate how close is Davis and Burns formulation (equation 1) from the exact worst case response time presented in this paper (equation 6). The two proposals coincide when the selected task to calculate its worst case response time belongs to the highest priority domain. However, as the number of domains increase, I (w n si ) < I(w n si ), since it does not have to be true that all domains cause the maximum interference in every activation. This effect is even more important when the selected task belongs to the lowest priority domain. Therefore, simulations have been done calculating the worst case response time of a task T di , being d the lowest priority domain of d total domains. Synthetic workload has been generated following the next rules: Number of domains d varies from 1 to 10. Number of tasks of each domain is 2; total utilisation of the entire system varies from 40% to 95%. For each utilisation, 10000 task sets have been generated, resulting in 550000 total simulations; domain periods varies from 5 to 50. Task periods varies from 50 to 500; the global algorithm used is Periodic Server; if the generated task set is not schedulable, then it is rejected.

The results are plotted in Figure 5. In this figure, the worst case response time obtained with Davis and Burns analysis is compared with our proposal against number of domains. As we expected, when there is only one domain, the two analysis give the same worst case response time but, as the number of domains increase, Davis and Burns bound moves away from the exact value. For the case of ten domains, deviation raises to about 25%.

div.head: VII. Conclusions
div.p: This paper points out that the exact worst case response time analysis for hierarchical fixed-priority scheduling by Davis and Burns [3] is only exact for tasks of the highest priority domain. For the rest of the tasks, it is an upper bound. In our work, we have provided the exact analysis. Simulations have shown that Davis and Burns analysis is very close to the exact formulation for systems with few domains. However, as the number of domains increase, the analysis becomes more pessimistic.

The exact analysis provided in this paper implies to assign different offsets to higher priority domains. The disadvantage is that, as the number of domains increase, it also increases the number of scenarios to check, which increases the cost of the algorithm. One of the future lines of work is to try to reduce the number of scenarios to reduce the cost of the algorithm.

Despite there has been growing attention to hierarchical scheduling in recent years, up until now, related works have mainly worked from a theoretical point of view. XtratuM hypervisor provides a framework to run several operating systems (or real-time executives) in a robust partitioned environment. One of our current research lines is to provide exact schedulability tests and implementing them in XtratuM. The ongoing work is focused on measuring the overhead introduced by these tests.
